items.stem: Why is accurate, synchronised time across log sources important for a SIEM?

options.text: Correlating events in the right order depends on consistent timestamps
options.rationale: Correct: skewed clocks break the sequencing that correlation relies on.
Time synchronisation does not reduce file size.
Clock sync is unrelated to encryption.

options.text: It removes the need for parsing
options.rationale: Parsing is still required regardless of time sync.

items.explanation: Correct: consistent timestamps let the SIEM order and correlate events.

items.stem: Which TWO are good ways to reduce false positives without hiding real threats? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Refine the rule logic to match the true attack pattern more precisely
options.rationale: Correct: tighter logic cuts noise while keeping real detections.

options.text: Exclude a specific, verified benign source with documentation
options.rationale: Correct: a documented, scoped exclusion reduces noise safely.
Disabling removes detection along with the noise.

options.text: Raise the threshold so high nothing ever alerts
options.rationale: An unreachable threshold hides genuine attacks.

items.explanation: Correct: precise logic and a documented, scoped exclusion both cut noise safely.

items.stem: A correlation rule fires on many failed logins followed by a success from the same source. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: A possible successful brute-force or password-guessing attack
options.rationale: Correct: repeated failures then success is a classic brute-force signature.

options.text: A printer running out of toner
options.rationale: Printing status is unrelated to login patterns.

options.text: A normal, expected login with no concern
options.rationale: The burst of failures makes this worth investigating.
Updates do not produce failed-then-successful logins.

items.explanation: Correct: failures followed by success suggests a brute-force that may have succeeded.
